title: IndiGo's Bhatia Slams India's Pilot Duty Rules as 'Uncompetitive,' Seeks Review
excerpt: IndiGo managing director Rahul Bhatia has called for an overhaul of India's flight duty time rules, arguing they erode cockpit productivity and drive up airline costs—months after the regulations triggered the worst scheduling crisis in Indian aviation history.
body:
• IndiGo MD Rahul Bhatia says revised pilot flight duty time rules reduce cockpit productivity and make Indian aviation "uncompetitive" compared with global peers.
  • The DGCA's revised FDTL norms, which took effect in November 2025, contributed to over 2,500 flight cancellations at IndiGo in December and a 15% stock plunge.
  • Bhatia also urges the government to rationalise ATF taxes and airport charges, noting that airport user fees have surged up to 95% in three years while airline fares rose just 1–3%.
  • IndiGo added 330 pilots in FY26 and is positioning international expansion as its next growth engine, with plans to reach 200 million passengers annually by FY30.

IndiGo co-founder and managing director Rahul Bhatia has launched one of the airline's sharpest public attacks on India's revised pilot flight duty time regulations, telling PTI in an interview that the norms have gutted cockpit productivity and placed Indian carriers at a structural disadvantage against global competitors.

"When you come up with a policy where the productivity in the cockpit diminishes to the extent it has, it makes Indian aviation uncompetitive. It directly impacts the cost structure."

— Rahul Bhatia, Managing Director, IndiGo

What Changed and Why It Hurt

The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) implemented revised Flight Duty Time Limitations (FDTL) in phases through 2025, with full enforcement from November 1. The new norms increased mandatory weekly pilot rest from 36 to 48 hours, capped night flying by limiting night landings to two per week (down from six), and revised duty period calculations to account for circadian rhythm and fatigue.

Pilot associations backed the changes as a long-pending safety measure, and the International Federation of Air Line Pilots' Associations (IFALPA) warned against any dilution. But IndiGo, which operates on a lean-staffing, high-utilisation model heavily reliant on night flights, was blindsided. Between December 2 and 12, 2025, the airline cancelled 2,507 flights over three days, stranding tens of thousands of passengers during the peak winter and wedding travel season.

The fallout was swift: InterGlobe Aviation's stock plunged roughly 15%, wiping ₹35,000–40,000 crore from the company's market capitalisation. The DGCA ordered a 10% cut in IndiGo's winter schedule and cited over-optimised operations, inadequate regulatory preparedness, and software deficiencies. A temporary exemption from the revised FDTL norms was granted until February 10, 2026. CEO Pieter Elbers resigned in March 2026, with Bhatia stepping in to oversee operations.

Bhatia's Case for Reform

Bhatia framed his criticism as a competitiveness argument, not a safety one. He told PTI that no airline wants unsafe operations, but India's rules overshoot global benchmarks.

"If India wants to compete with the world, then one cannot have FDTL regulations that are so far off the mark from global benchmarks that it actually drives a deep wedge into your efficiency."

— Rahul Bhatia, Managing Director, IndiGo

Describing aviation as a "fine margin" business, Bhatia said every incremental cost matters. He pointed to U.S. flight duty rules as a reference, noting it would be "unfair" to suggest American FDTL standards are less safe than India's. IndiGo's FY26 annual report, released this week, acknowledged that the revised crew rostering rules posed "execution challenges" during a peak travel period, contributing to delays, service disruptions, and cancellations.

Cost Pressures Pile Up

The FDTL critique came alongside a broader push by Bhatia for the government to rationalise aviation taxes. He argued that aviation turbine fuel (ATF) taxes and airport charges continue to treat air travel "as if it's an elitist mode of transport," when it has effectively become a public utility.

Over the past three years, airport User Development Fee (UDF) charges have surged by up to 95%, and landing and parking charges have risen by as much as 34%, according to Bhatia. Meanwhile, fares retained by airlines have increased by only 1–3%, even as inflation climbed roughly 12%. ATF accounts for about 40% of an airline's operating costs, and no Indian airline currently hedges jet fuel prices, Bhatia said.

InterGlobe Aviation posted a record consolidated net loss of ₹2,394 crore for FY26, even as operating revenue rose 5% year-on-year to ₹84,962 crore and the airline carried over 130 million passengers.

Expansion Despite Turbulence

Despite the financial and regulatory headwinds, IndiGo is pressing ahead with an aggressive growth strategy. The airline added 330 pilots in FY26, ending the year with 5,786 pilots and a total workforce of 41,907. It plans to hire another 1,000 pilots to support expansion. As of June 30, 2026, IndiGo operated 432 aircraft across 97 domestic and 46 international destinations, commanding a 66.3% domestic market share.

The FY26 annual report positions international operations as the airline's next major growth driver. During the year, IndiGo launched long-haul services to the United Kingdom and Eastern Europe, inducted the Airbus A321XLR, and commenced direct flights to Athens. The airline targets 200 million passengers annually by FY30, up from 123 million in FY26, with plans to expand its fleet to over 550 aircraft and increase daily departures to around 3,000.

For the Indian diaspora, particularly those flying frequently between India and destinations in Europe, the UK, and the Middle East, IndiGo's long-haul push could eventually offer more direct and competitively priced routing options—provided the airline can resolve its regulatory and operational challenges first.

What's Next

Bhatia said conversations with the government on FDTL reform are ongoing. The Delhi High Court is also hearing a contempt petition by the Indian Pilots Guild alleging the DGCA granted unauthorised exemptions from the norms, and the Competition Commission of India is examining IndiGo's market dominance following the December disruptions. With pilot unions, courts, and regulators all engaged, any loosening of duty rules will face significant pushback—even as India's largest airline insists the current framework is holding back the world's fastest-growing aviation market.
nri_angle: IndiGo's aggressive international expansion—including new long-haul routes to the UK, Europe, and plans for A350 widebody service—could offer diaspora travellers more direct, competitively priced connections to India, but regulatory and operational challenges remain.
